set.statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about 1 to 2 hours before death, every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) found, where a published source gave both values for the same case, median ratios to femoral blood across drugs of 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with differences of more than tenfold between drugs (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no range or interval is given for any ratio, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the first sample was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 98 substances and prints a single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratio for 82 of them, none for THC, without case numbers or per-drug sources (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of the 24 drugs with a value in both, its ratio is more than 10% above the compilation's paired median for other blood, which is not only heart blood (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In bodies examined after death, the amount of a drug often depended on which blood vessel the blood came from: in four overdose deaths it differed about 3 to 7 times for the drugs taken in the overdose, usually higher near the heart, lungs and liver than in the thigh. In one person tested in hospital before death, every sample taken after death was about 2 to 8 times higher. In a collection of about 5,000 cases from many studies, blood from other places, such as the heart, typically held about a quarter more drug than thigh blood, and the gap differed more than tenfold between drugs. In bodies tested more than once, thigh-blood levels rose after death for some drugs and fell for others, and the first test was often many hours after death. So a level after death can make a drug look more, or less, involved than it was. Most of this comes from small or selected studies, mostly of medicines, and how much a level changes in an ordinary death is not known.
set.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Paired median ratios to femoral blood across drugs (number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Single heart-to-peripheral ratios without case numbers (narrative review; printed for 82 of 98 substances): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No intervals anywhere.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them focused on poisonings, without appraisal, weighting or spread (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

evidence_set: Limitations stated by the authors: some published studies focus on intoxications, with high concentrations in tissue and femoral blood, while others show normal variation regardless of cause of death; cases could not be classified by cause of death because it was not always given; time since death was not always given and can range from a few hours to months; the femoral concentrations in Tables 2 and 5 are usually higher than the all-cause reference medians; co-ingested drugs, metabolism, genetic background, age, disease and the circumstances of death were mostly not given; some drug–specimen ratios rest on few results and are only suggestive; sampling site and procedure vary between cases.

Paragraph beginning 'The cardiac to peripheral blood level' (p. 48, right column); Table 2 (p. 49); sentence introducing Table 2 at the end of the paragraph beginning 'Recent studies have demonstrated' (p. 48, continuing on p. 50)

Heart-to-peripheral blood ratios are offered as a measure of the potential for change after death, with high ratios meaning heart samples may overstate concentrations. Table 2, titled as drugs in which transformation or redistribution after death may occur, has 99 entries for 98 substances (venlafaxine twice) and prints an approximate ratio for 82; 16 have none, among them THC, pentobarbital, lidocaine and four fentanyl analogues. Examples: amphetamine 2.0, methamphetamine 2.4 (D-methamphetamine 2.1), MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3, morphine (heroin) 2.2, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, diazepam 1.6, doxepin 5.5. No case numbers, no spread (except the ranges for cocaine and imipramine) and no per-drug sources; the table is cited collectively to refs 14, 15 and 20–33. Editors' comparison with the paired other-blood medians of Ketola & Kriikku (2019, Table 3): of the 24 drugs with a value in both, this review's ratio is more than 10% higher for 17 (for example morphine 2.2 against 1.26, methamphetamine 2.4 against 1.50, oxycodone 3.1 against 1.19), lower for 3 (chloroquine, clozapine, fluoxetine) and within 10% for 4 (metoprolol, oxazepam, promethazine, venlafaxine); other blood in the compilation is not only heart blood, and peripheral blood here is not necessarily femoral.

set.statement: A drug concentration measured after death cannot on its own show that the drug caused the death: concentrations in deaths put down to a drug overlap with those in deaths from other causes and with the reference ranges of living patients taking the drug as a treatment, tolerance shifts the level a person can survive, and levels change after death (see the answer on whether levels change after death). In Finland, where police can order a medico-legal investigation of a sudden or unexplained death and the forensic pathologist decides whether to test for drugs (over 13% of all deaths), one laboratory measured femoral-blood levels in 57,903 deaths of all causes with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, sampled on average five days after death; for 46 of 129 drugs the median level was above the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical reference list, by up to 100-fold for one drug (24-fold for the next), for 61 it was within that range and for 22 below it. The median for methadone (207 deaths) and for buprenorphine (671 deaths) lay within the treatment range although forensic pathologists certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings with that drug as the main finding, and the authors state that for strong opioids the level after death plays a somewhat limited part in judging the cause, as it partly does for amphetamine and other drugs to which tolerance develops; the medians mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out levels too low to measure, and compare whole blood with plasma ranges (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Among deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England (1992 to 2008), femoral-blood MDMA overlapped widely between deaths put down to MDMA (0.478 to 53.9 mg/L in 13 with a value) and deaths from injuries (0.035 to 4.81 mg/L in 24), although the median was about 7 times higher in the first group (editors' calculation; Milroy, 2011; see the answer on MDMA levels). A 1977 Michigan series, as a 1996 narrative review describes it, found blood morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes, such as injuries or homicide, in 74% of deaths put down to heroin overdose (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand; see the answer on heroin 'overdoses'). A clinical pharmacologist's review adds, second-hand, that published 'lethal' ranges are wide and overlap (for example 40 to 8,500 µg/L quoted for MDMA and 60 to 3,100 µg/L for methadone), that amounts that would kill a person without tolerance are survived by people who use heroin regularly, and that a fatal level could only be defined by classing deaths as caused by the drug or not without knowing the measured levels and then comparing the two groups (Ferner, 2008), which none of the studies read here reports doing; a 2003 practitioners' review lists nine questions a toxicologist should answer before judging a drug's role, among them where the blood was taken, whether the drug changes after death, what is known of the person's tolerance and whether the autopsy findings fit (Leikin & Watson, 2003). Both directions follow: a level that looks high can lead to a death being put down to a drug that was only present, and an ordinary or low level does not rule a drug out. A study of whether drugs were present, not of their levels, shows that judging without a full autopsy also errs both ways: at one North Carolina centre that kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths (2016 to 2021), 265 of 2,719 deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug deaths (9.75%) were given a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology (by the paper's definition, deaths with no drug found or with drugs present but another sufficient cause; the split is not reported), while 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were judged drug deaths; the pathologists counted any illicit drug found as at least contributing unless a catastrophic other cause was found (Hancock et al., 2024; see the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing). In the Finnish and North Carolina studies the forensic pathologists who decided the cause had the case's toxicology results; the Sheffield and Michigan reports, as read here, do not say who decided the causes or whether the levels were known. None of the studies read here itself compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment; the heroin review cites three comparisons with survivors of overdose, without figures. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Can a blood test after death show that a drug caused the death? Not on its own. In Finland, in about 58,000 deaths tested for drugs (2000 to 2010), the usual level after death was higher than the treatment level of living patients for 46 of 129 drugs. For methadone and buprenorphine the usual level was in the treatment range, even though more than 4 in 10 of those deaths were counted as poisonings mainly by that drug, and people who use heroin regularly can survive amounts that would kill someone without tolerance. In an English study, MDMA levels in deaths blamed on MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries, and an old US study, as a review reports it, found the same for morphine in deaths blamed on heroin. So a high level can lead to a death being blamed on a drug that was only there, and a normal level does not rule a drug out. At one US centre, a full autopsy found another cause for about 1 in 10 deaths first thought to be drug deaths, while about half of the deaths not suspected turned out to be drug deaths. In Finland and at the US centre, the doctors who decided the causes had the test results.
set.magnitude: Finland 2000–2010 (57,903 deaths; 129 drugs): median femoral concentration above the therapeutic plasma range for 46 drugs (printed 35%; 35.7%, editors' calculation), within for 61 (47%), below for 22 (17%); with the stated rule applied consistently, about 48, 58 and 23 (editors' calculation on the card); largest ratio to the upper therapeutic limit 100 (hydroxychloroquine), next 24 (promazine). Methadone median 0.40 mg/L (therapeutic 0.1–0.5), 43% certified as poisonings with methadone as the main finding; buprenorphine 0.0012 mg/L (0.0005–0.005), 45%; morphine 0.07 mg/L (0.01–0.1), 4%. Sheffield 1992–2008: MDMA deaths 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49; n = 13), injury deaths 0.035–4.81 mg/L (median 0.483; n = 24); at least 7 of the 13 inside the injury range (editors' calculation). Michigan 1977 (second-hand): 74% of heroin overdose deaths with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes. Quoted lethal ranges (second-hand): MDMA 40–8,500 µg/L, methadone 60–3,100 µg/L. North Carolina 2016–2021 (presence, not levels): 265/2,719 (9.75%) suspected drug deaths with a non-drug final cause; 115/237 (48.5%, editors' calculation) of deaths not suspected judged drug deaths. No intervals.
set.comparator: Therapeutic plasma reference ranges for living patients; deaths with the same drug present but another cause; deaths not certified as poisoning by the drug; the final cause after full autopsy
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: In Finland and North Carolina the causes of death were assigned by forensic pathologists who had the case's toxicology results, and the Sheffield and Michigan reports do not say who assigned them or what was known, which can build part of any difference between groups into the comparison; the Finnish medians mix poisonings with other deaths and leave out levels too low to measure (card sc_launiainen_2014, JBI moderate); the MDMA groups are small and their certifiers unnamed (card sc_milroy_2011, JBI high); the heroin figure is second-hand; the North Carolina reference standard counts illicit drugs present as contributing (card sc_hancock_2024, JBI moderate).
set.population: Deaths with drugs measured after death: 57,903 Finnish medico-legal autopsies of all causes with full drug testing, 2000–2010; Sheffield autopsies with MDMA or a related drug, 1992–2008 (13 deaths put down to MDMA and 24 injury deaths with a femoral-blood value); deaths put down to heroin overdose in a 1977 Michigan series (second-hand); 2,956 autopsies at one North Carolina centre, 2016–2021
